project.title: The Bell That Never Rang
project.ai_instructions: Plant fair clues before the solution and never introduce decisive information only at the reveal. Keep Ritsu's observations concise and separate inference from fact. Give every suspect a reason to lie beyond murder, and keep the crime-night times and object movements consistent.

tree_nodes.title: Part One: The Silent Bell
tree_nodes.synopsis: A changed will and a death in a locked room on a storm night.

tree_nodes.title: Chapter One: The Storm Invitation
tree_nodes.synopsis: Ritsu Otonashi arrives at Bellmist Manor to edit a memoir. The housekeeper says the bell cannot ring tonight.

tree_nodes.title: Chapter Two: The Last Dinner
tree_nodes.synopsis: Soichiro Kurose announces a new will. Toma pours tea into Soichiro's private celadon cup.

tree_nodes.synopsis: A bell sounds twelve times at 11:50. At 12:10 Soichiro is found in the locked study.

tree_nodes.synopsis: Ritsu reframes the locked room as a question of what the victim swallowed before entering.
tree_nodes.content: {"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The next morning Ritsu measured the bell-tower study. The door had a spring latch. Once Soichiro entered and locked it from inside, no killer needed to leave the room."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Even so, Mio found "},{"type":"text","text":"a brass spare key","marks":[{"type":"foreshadowSetup","attrs":{"setupId":"sample-setup-key","foreshadowId":"sample-foreshadow-key"}}]},{"type":"text","text":" inside a blue book of poems. It was not the house key Maho had used."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"In the bell mechanism room, the rope had been removed and the striking hammer clamped in place. The tower bell could not physically have rung the night before."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Salt marked the window ledge, and a single flake of dry mud lay on the floor. Both clues looked too carefully arranged to prove an escape."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Ritsu removed the locked room from the problem of exits. The question was what Soichiro had swallowed before he turned the key."}]}]}

chat_sessions.title: Making the celadon cup a fair clue

chat_messages.content: I want the celadon cup to be a clue only the killer could exploit, but I do not want it to look suspicious on first reading. How much should I describe?

Describe its color and chipped rim once, and place the person pouring the tea in the same paragraph. Let dialogue establish that only Soichiro uses it. Do not mention poison or medicine. On rereading, the reader can see how one drink was targeted.
Is putting Toma's name in the same paragraph too strong?
It would be strong in isolation, but serving tea is ordinary. Immediately add other suspicious actions—Mio leaving, Chikage watching his color—so attention is divided fairly.
All four witnesses lie. I want each to remain a suspect, but I need the lies to feel different.

Give each lie a different object. Mio lies about place, Chikage about professional responsibility, Maho about the house's past, and Toma about time. Only the time lie reaches the murder, but every lie is worth hiding to its owner.
I also want Matrix to show how each witness relates to the scene.

Split Chapter Five into four Beats and assign each Beat a POV or target character. Then the prose structure and Matrix intersections reinforce one another; the testimony itself becomes the feature demonstration.
Does poisoning him at dinner and letting him enter the locked room himself make the locked-room mystery feel weak?

It creates a classical reversal: the reader assumes the killer had to leave. Seed the spare key as a red herring, but establish the spring latch and self-locking sequence early so the solution is not withheld information.
When should I reveal the bell recording?

Reveal the phonograph in Part One, but keep the cylinder's contents until the final chapter. First establish the impossible condition—the real bell cannot ring—then delay only the substitute source, leaving the reader room to infer it.

foreshadows.title: The Severed Bell Rope
foreshadows.intent: Establish that the real bell cannot sound, then use that impossibility to prove the recording in the final chapter.
foreshadows.notes: Planted in the housekeeper's line in Chapter One; paid off in the final chapter.

foreshadows.title: The Celadon Cup
foreshadows.intent: Plant the one cup that lets the killer target Soichiro's drink without making the service look unnatural.
foreshadows.notes: Planted at dinner; paid off as the poison route.

foreshadows.title: The Stopped Pocket Watch
foreshadows.intent: Preserve the actual collapse time, 11:47, and put it in conflict with the false midnight.
foreshadows.notes: Found with the body; resolves the true time of death.

foreshadows.title: The Brass Spare Key
foreshadows.intent: A red herring for the locked room that explains Mio's separate lie but not the murder.
foreshadows.notes: Found in Chapter Four; ruled unused in the solution.

foreshadows.title: The 11:50 Bell
foreshadows.intent: Make a heard sound look like proof of time, then reverse it into a phonograph performance.

snippets.title: The Bell at 11:50
snippets.content:
At eleven fifty, a low bell sounded twelve times somewhere in the manor.

Only Toma insisted on the direction of the sound.

snippets.title: Ritsu's Observation Rule
snippets.content:
Number facts. Put question marks after inferences.

When several witnesses repeat the same wording, suspect guidance rather than memory.

snippets.title: The Celadon Cup
snippets.content:
Five white cups. At Soichiro's place alone, a chipped celadon cup.

Ask not only who drank, but who alone could drink from it.
